A Uniform Type Ia Supernova Distance Ladder with the Zwicky Transient Facility:
Absolute Calibration Based on the Tip of the Red Giant Branch (TRGB) Method

California Blvd, Pasadena, CA 91125, USA
Abstract

The current Cepheid-calibrated distance ladder measurement of H0H_{0} is reported to be in tension with the values inferred from the cosmic microwave background (CMB), assuming standard cosmology. However, some tip of the red giant branch (TRGB) estimates report H0H_{0} in better agreement with the CMB. Hence, it is critical to reduce systematic uncertainties in local measurements to understand the Hubble tension. In this paper, we propose a uniform distance ladder between the second and third rungs, combining SNe Ia observed by the Zwicky Transient Facility (ZTF) with a TRGB calibration of their absolute luminosity. A large, volume-limited sample of both calibrator and Hubble flow SNe Ia from the same survey minimizes two of the largest sources of systematics: host-galaxy bias and non-uniform photometric calibration. We present results from a pilot study using existing TRGB distance to the host galaxy of ZTF SN Ia SN 2021rhu (aka ZTF21abiuvdk) in NGC7814. Combining the ZTF calibrator with a volume-limited sample from the first data release of ZTF Hubble flow SNe Ia, we infer H0=76.94±6.4​km​s−1​Mpc−1H_{0}=76.94\pm 6.4\,{\rm km}\,{\rm s^{-1}}\,{\rm Mpc^{-1}}, an 8.3%8.3\% measurement. The error budget is dominated by the single object calibrating the SN Ia luminosity in this pilot study. However, the ZTF sample includes already five other SNe Ia within ∼\sim 20 Mpc for which TRGB distances can be obtained with HST. Finally, we present the prospects of building this distance ladder out to 80 Mpc with JWST observations of more than one hundred ZTF SNe Ia.

Keywords: 
cosmology: observations - supernovae

I Introduction

In recent years, a remarkable increase in accuracy obtained by a broad range of independent cosmological observations has provided compelling support for our current standard Λ\Lambda cold dark matter (Λ\LambdaCDM) model. This concordance cosmology successfully explains the measurements of fluctuations in the temperature and polarization of the cosmic microwave background (CMB) radiation [52] as well as observations of large-scale structure and matter fluctuations in the universe, e.g. baryon acoustic oscillations [41, BAO;].

With improved accuracy of recent observations, some discrepancies have been noted. The prima facie most significant tension is between the CMB inferred value of the Hubble constant (H0H_{0}) and the direct measurement of its local value [56]. The local measurements are based on a calibration of the absolute luminosity of Type Ia supernovae (SNe Ia) using independent distances to host galaxies of nearby SNe Ia, known as the “cosmic distance ladder”. This claimed tension, if confirmed, it could provide evidence for of new fundamental physics beyond the standard model of cosmology. It could, however, be a sign of unknown sources of systematic error. Currently, the local H0H_{0} methods have slight differences in their values. The tip of the red giant branch [21, TRGB;] and Cepheid [56] distance scales yield values of 69.8 ±\pm 1.7 [however, see also, 5, for, e.g.] and 73.04 ±\pm 1.04 kms−1​Mpc−1{\rm s}^{-1}{\rm Mpc}^{-1}, respectively. Understanding these differences is important to discern whether the tension is a sign of novel physics or a yet-to-be-revealed systematic error. To date, only the TRGB and Cepheid measurements have measured distances to ten or more host galaxies of SNe Ia.

Circumventing the two largest known sources of systematic error is key to achieving the percent level precision in the local distance scale and resolving the Hubble tension. Firstly, Cepheid variables strongly prefer young, star-forming environments. This has been shown to bias the inferred SN Ia luminosity, and hence H0H_{0} [58], though the size of this effect is currently debated [33]. While the current Cepheid distance ladder, consisting of SNe Ia within a 40  Mpc volume in young, star forming hosts [56], addresses this issue by evaluating H0H_{0} from only the Hubble flow SNe Ia in low stellar mass hosts, it is important to measure H0H_{0} using a volume-limited calibrator and Hubble flow sample of SNe Ia in all types of host galaxies, to quantify the environment dependent biases, given the profound cosmological implications of the Hubble tension. TRGB stars, unlike Cepheid variables, are found in both old and young environments, hence they can probe SN Ia host galaxies of all morphological types in a given volume. The TRGB is a well-understood standard candle, arising from the core helium flash luminosity at the end phase of red giant branch (RGB) evolution for low-mass stars [22, 32, 21]. Furthermore, TRGB stars, found in the outskirts of galaxies, are less prone than Cepheids to biases from crowding, and are also comparatively less sensitive to reddening systematics, a potential contribution to the Cepheid H0H_{0} measurements [44, e.g.,].

Secondly, the current sample of SNe Ia for H0H_{0} measurements is derived from several (>20>20) different combinations of telescopes, instruments and filters [60, 56, e.g.]. Although there have been significant efforts to cross-calibrate the heterogeneous systems [7], there are irreducible uncertainties associated with the data where the filters, instruments and even telescopes no longer exist. In light of these outstanding sources of error, it is beneficial to have a volume limited sample of calibrator and Hubble flow SNe Ia observed with the same instrument.

Addressing these issues, here we present a uniform distance ladder, with both calibrator and Hubble flow SNe Ia observed by the Zwicky Transient Facility [2, 26, ZTF;], calibrated on the basis of the TRGB method. As both the calibrator and Hubble flow rungs of the distance ladder are observed with the same instrument, we only rely on a relative photometric calibration, which is a significantly simpler task than controlling the absolute calibration of an SN Ia sample. In this pilot study, we present ZTF calibrator SNe Ia within a nearby volume of luminosity distance, DL<20D_{L}<20 Mpc and measure preliminary distances, where possible, for those SNe Ia using the tip of the red giant branch. In the long term, we need a ZTF calibrator sample of ∼\sim 100 SNe Ia to get to ∼1%\sim 1\% precision and accuracy on H0H_{0} (assuming the current precision in the TRGB absolute magnitude calibration) to resolve the tension. With the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) scheduled to start taking data in mid-2022, we can feasibly extend the calibrator rung to DL∼80D_{L}\sim 80\,Mpc. ZTF has already observed well-sampled light curves for more than one hundred SNe Ia in this distance range. Therefore, within the DL≤80D_{L}\leq 80\,Mpc volume we will no longer be limited by the rate of SNe Ia in galaxies to obtain calibrator distances, currently a limiting factor for the largest calibrator sample [56].

II Data and methodology

We present the data for SNe Ia observed by ZTF in a DL<20D_{L}<20 Mpc volume, for which there are sufficient observations to infer a distance from the TRGB method. While 5 SNe Ia have adequate light curve sampling to get precise peak magnitudes, shape and color parameters from SNe Ia, only one of them, ZTF21abiuvdk (aka SN 2021rhu) has observations of the host galaxy to get an accurate distance.

SN 2021rhu exploded in NGC 7814 (see Figure 1, left inset), at α=0.8143∘,δ=16.1457∘\alpha=0.8143^{\circ},\delta=16.1457^{\circ} (J2000 coordinates), classified as a SN Ia on the Transient Name Server [45, 61, TNS;]. We obtained photometry with a 1-day cadence for SN 2021rhu with ZTF, in the g,r,ig,r,i filters between −14.1-14.1 and +172.5 days. These observations begin on 2021-07-01.4 UTC. Hence, we obtained a densely sampled light curve with the ZTF observing system [15], in multiple filters, i.e., the same system as the Hubble flow sample [16, as presented in]. The images were processed with the pipeline as detailed in Masci et al. [43]. The lightcurve, thus far, spans a large phase range from 2021-07-01.4 to 2021-11-11.11 (Figure 3 shows the range used in the fit). We have also obtained a well-sampled spectral time series, beginning with a classification spectrum with the SEDmachine [4, 57, 37] on 2021-07-05. These are presented in detail in a companion paper (Harvey et al. in prep). Figure 3 shows a maximum-light spectrum obtained with the SPectrograph for the Rapid Acquisition of Transients [50, SPRAT;] on the Liverpool Telescope [62, LT;].

SNe Ia distances are inferred from light curve peak luminosity, shape and color. The most widely used light-curve fitting algorithm, which we adopt for our analysis, is the Spectral Adaptive Lightcurve Template - 2 [27, SALT2;]. This model treats the color entirely empirically, without distinguishing the intrinsic and extrinsic components. We use the most updated, published version of SALT2 [28, 3, SALT2.4, see] as implemented in sncosmo v2.1.011 1 https://sncosmo.readthedocs.io/en/v2.1.x/ [1], identical to the lightcurve inference of the Hubble flow sample in [16]. In the fitting procedure, we correct the SN fluxes for extinction due to dust in the Milky Way (MW). Extinction values for the SN coordinates derived in Schlafly & Finkbeiner [59] were applied, using the galactic reddening law proposed in [12], with a total-to-selective absorption ratio, RV=3.1R_{V}=3.1, the canonical MW value.

II.1 TRGB distance estimate

NGC 7814 was observed with the Advanced Camera for Surveys (ACS) on HST (see Figure 1) covering a total of seven fields as part of the GHOSTS survey [54]. Here, we reanalyse the data using a pipeline by the Carnegie-Chicago Hubble Program [22, CCHP;] which implements its own point-spread function (PSF) fitting photometry based on DOLPHOT [17] modeling synthetic PSFs with TinyTim [38].

The details of the pipeline can be found in Jang et al. [32]. We select fields 3, 4, and 5 from the entire dataset since fields 1 and 2 are close to the disk of the galaxy and hence susceptible to high crowding and extinction biases, whereas fields 6 and 7 are very sparse making it difficult to identify the TRGB. We perform artificial star tests, as a robustness test of the photometric pipeline, by injecting ∼\sim200,000 stars into the FLC images and recover them using DOLPHOT. The artificial stars have a similar colors range to blue RGB stars in the shaded region of the CMD (see Figure 2). We populate stars within a brightness range of 25<F​814​W≤2925<F814W\leq 29 mag. To mimic the observed spatial distribution and luminosity function (LF), we place more stars in the inner region of the galaxy.

The LF was binned with a width of 0.01 mag and smoothed with a Gaussian kernel of 0.1 mag (e.g. Figure 2). The edge detection is derived from the first derivative of the scale smoothed LF [see 29, for details]. We perform a tip detection on each individual field and find the values to be consistent within errors and hence, take the average of the individual measurements with a conservative error for the TRGB. We find a Milky Way extinction corrected tip at F​814​W0,TRGB=26.81±0.06F814W_{0,\rm TRGB}=26.81\pm 0.06 mag.22 2 Data associated with Figure 2 can be found in https://github.com/hanlbomi/NGC7814-Field4 Details of the tests, the impact of assumptions on the various components of the pipeline and consistency between the individual fields and with distances reported in the literature are presented in a companion paper (Jang et al. 2022 in prep). Inferring the distance to NGC 7814 from this tip measurement requires an absolute calibration of the TRGB magnitude. We use the most recent absolute calibration of the TRGB magnitude that is derived from multiple primary anchors, namely MW, LMC. SMC and NGC 4258, from Freedman [21], MF814WTRGB=−4.049±0.038M_{\rm F814W}^{\rm TRGB}=-4.049\pm 0.038 [see also, 39, for a new calibration from the Milky Way] and we obtain a distance modulus of μ=30.86±0.07\mu=30.86\pm 0.07 mag. The individual sources of error in the final distance uncertainty are presented in Table 1. We note that there is debate in the literature regarding the value of this absolute magnitude, depending on the assumptions in the primary anchors. The TRGB magnitude can be calibrated using the parallax distances from the Gaia satellite early data release 3 [24] to Milky Way (MW) globular clusters, e.g. ω\omega Cen, detached eclipsing binary distances to the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds [51, 25, LMC, SMC] and the water maser distance to the nearby galaxy NGC 4258 [55]. The difference assumptions / anchor combinations have led to a difference of up to ∼0.1\sim 0.1 mag in the inferred absolute magnitude. A summary of the various absolute calibrations in the literature are provided in Blakeslee et al. [5], Freedman [21].

We combine the calibrator data with the ZTF DR1 Hubble flow sample [16]. TRGB stars are found in all types of SN Ia host galaxies and therefore, the TRGB-calibrated sample will be volume limited. To have a completely volume-limited distance ladder, i.e. both calibrator and Hubble flow rungs, in this study, we also only fit the volume-limited Hubble flow sample from ZTF DR1. However, we note that the ZTF Hubble flow SN Ia sample has been built with carefully controlled selection function via the Bright Transient Survey [23, 48, e.g.,]. In future studies, this will be a unique advantage since we can use this to compute the selection effects for SNe Ia with redshifts up to z∼0.1z\sim 0.1, where the impact of peculiar velocity errors is significantly lower than for literature samples [see 16, for details]. For this study, since we are dominated in the uncertainty budget by having only a single calibrator, we conservatively take the sample to be complete to z≤0.06z\leq 0.06. This selection cut reduces the Hubble flow sample from 200 to 98 SNe Ia.

III Results

We fit the SALT2 light-curve model to the calibrator SN and get the peak luminosity, light-curve width and color. We note that since SALT2 is not well defined at wavelengths redder than 7000 Å, we only fit the gg and rr filters [34, e.g.]. SN 2021rhu has SALT2 parameters mB=12.22±0.033m_{B}=12.22\pm 0.033, light-curve shape x1=−2.074±0.025x_{1}=-2.074\pm 0.025, and color, c=0.054±0.028c=0.054\pm 0.028. While the x1x_{1} and cc are within the range of typical cosmological cuts (e.g., |x1|<3|x_{1}|<3, |c|<0.3|c|<0.3), it has a low x1x_{1} value which is also seen in peculiar, fast-declining SNe Ia. However, the light curves of SN 2021rhu show a clear shoulder in the rr band and a second peak in the ii band (Figure 3), characteristic of normal and transitional SNe Ia used for cosmology [31]. We also compute the color-stretch parameter, sB​Vs_{BV}, with the SNooPY method, since it is shown to be better at parametrizing the fast declining SNe Ia [10]. We find sBV=0.72s_{\rm BV}=0.72 consistent with normal/transitional SNe Ia, appropriate to use for cosmology [11]. It is also spectroscopically similar to transitional SNe Ia like SN 2011iv [20], which have been used for estimating H0H_{0} [22], thus this object is consistent with the cosmological sample of SNe Ia.

Here, we present the formalism for inferring H0H_{0}. The absolute magnitude of SNe Ia, MBM_{B}, is given by

mB0−μhost=MBm_{B}^{0}-\mu_{\rm host}=M_{B} (1)

where mB0{m}_{B}^{0} is the standardized apparent peak magnitude of the SN Ia and μhost\mu_{\rm host} is the distance modulus to the host galaxy based on the TRGB method. The Hubble flow SNe Ia measure the intercept of the magnitude-redshift relation, aBa_{B}. Ignoring higher order terms, the intercept is given by

aB=log⁡c​z+log⁡[1+(1−q0)​z2−(1−q0−3​q02+j0)​z26]−0.2​mB0.\resizebox{20575110}{}{ $a_{B}=\log cz+\log\left[1+\frac{(1-q_{0})z}{2}-\frac{(1-q_{0}-3q^{2}_{0}+j_{0})z^{2}}{6}\right]-0.2m_{B}^{0}$}. (2)

We fix q0q_{0}, j0j_{0}, the deceleration and cosmic jerk parameters to the standard values of −0.55-0.55 and 1 respectively, since the low-zz SN Ia sample alone cannot constrain them. We note that while cosmological studies with SNe Ia correct the redshifts for the Hubble flow sample accounting for peculiar motion due to local large scale structure, this effect has been shown to be a sub-dominant source of error in measuring H0H_{0} [49], which is especially true here since only a single calibrator dominates the error budget. Additionally, we note that while this effect can be important when the calibrator sample is increased, as we have mentioned above, there will also be a simultaneous increase both in the size and the median redshift of the Hubble flow sample. mB0m_{B}^{0} is expressed in terms of the light-curve parameters and corrections as

mB0=mB+α​x1−β​c−δμ−biasm_{B}^{0}=m_{B}+\alpha x_{1}-\beta c-\delta_{\mu-{\rm bias}} (3)

where α\alpha and β\beta are the slopes of the width-luminosity and color-luminosity relations, respectively, and δμ−bias\delta_{\mu-{\rm bias}} is the bias correction needed to account for selection effects and other sources of distance bias. Following the formalism of Brout et al. [8], the canonical term for the host galaxy “mass-step” correction is absorbed in the bias correction δμ−bias\delta_{\mu-{\rm bias}} [6, see also]. Since both the calibrator described by equation 1 and the Hubble flow SNe Ia described by equation 2 are constructed to be volume-limited, such that they both have the same mass-step correction, the δμ−bias\delta_{\mu-{\rm bias}} term will cancel out.

The error for each SN includes fit uncertainty from the SALT2 covariance matrix (σfit\sigma_{\rm fit}), the peculiar velocity error (σpec\sigma_{\rm pec}) and σint\sigma_{\rm int}.

σm2=σfit2+σpec2+σint2\sigma^{2}_{\rm m}=\sigma^{2}_{\rm fit}+\sigma^{2}_{\rm pec}+\sigma^{2}_{\rm int} (4)

For σpec\sigma_{\rm pec} we derive the magnitude error from a velocity error of 300 km  s-1 [13]. We use PyMultiNest [9], a python wrapper for MultiNest [18] to derive the posterior distribution on the parameters. With the current calibrator, we find, H0=76.94±6.4​km​s−1​Mpc−1H_{0}=76.94\pm 6.4\,{\rm km}\,{\rm s^{-1}}\,{\rm Mpc^{-1}} . We also fit for H0H_{0} using the entire Hubble flow DR1 sample and find H0=77.60±6.0​km​s−1​Mpc−1H_{0}=77.60\pm 6.0\,{\rm km}\,{\rm s^{-1}}\,{\rm Mpc^{-1}}, a small difference of 0.66​km​s−1​Mpc−10.66\,{\rm km}\,{\rm s^{-1}}\,{\rm Mpc^{-1}}. This uncertainty is not significantly smaller when using the entire gold sample for ZTF DR1 compared to the volume limited one. This is because the main source of uncertainty is from having on a single calibrator object.

We also infer the corrected peak magnitudes with SNooPy [10]. While SNooPy uses a light-curve template, as opposed to a spectral template for SALT2, it is trained with a larger sample of transitional SNe Ia similar to SN 2021rhu, hence we compare H0H_{0} values from both methods. We compute distances to both the Hubble flow SNe Ia and SN 2021rhu with the EBV_model2. Using the same analysis method as for the SALT2 fitted distances, we infer an H0H_{0} value of 77.58±6.1​km​s−1​Mpc−177.58\pm 6.1\,{\rm km}\,{\rm s^{-1}}\,{\rm Mpc^{-1}}, a difference of 0.64​km​s−1​Mpc−10.64\,{\rm km}\,{\rm s^{-1}}\,{\rm Mpc^{-1}} from the value using SALT2. This difference is significantly smaller than the uncertainty on H0H_{0} from either method. Moreover, since SNooPy has a well-sampled training set to build the ii-band template, we also infer H0H_{0} from the g,r,ig,r,i filter combination and find a value of 76.17±6.0​km​s−1​Mpc−176.17\pm 6.0\,{\rm km}\,{\rm s^{-1}}\,{\rm Mpc^{-1}}, a difference of 0.77 km​s−1​Mpc−1{\rm km}\,{\rm s^{-1}}\,{\rm Mpc^{-1}} from the fiducial case.

IV Discussion and Conclusion

We present an estimate of H0H_{0} from a uniform distance ladder using the same survey for the calibrator sample as a homogeneous, untargeted Hubble flow sample. We use a TRGB distance to a nearby host galaxy of an SN Ia with high-cadence data in the ZTF g,r,ig,r,i filters. The current uncertainty is not sufficient to weigh in on the Hubble tension. We note that even a factor of 2 reduction in the Hubble flow sample by imposing the volume limit does not impact the uncertainty on H0H_{0}; the error currently is driven by having only a single ZTF SNe Ia with robust, independent distances. However, this can be increased with HST observations for nearby host galaxies. In the DL<20D_{L}<20 Mpc volume, one where we can achieve completeness relatively quickly, ZTF has observed 5 more spectroscopically normal SNe Ia with well-sampled light curves, a sample expected to increase by ∼1−2\sim 1-2 per year for the remainder of ZTF operations. These SNe are

  1. 1.

    ZTF19aacgslb (SN 2019np) in NGC 3254

  2. 2.

    ZTF20abijfqq (SN 2020nlb) in NGC 4382 (M85)

  3. 3.

    ZTF20abrjmgi (SN 2020qxp) in NGC 5002

  4. 4.

    ZTF21aaabvit (SN 2021J) in NGC 4414

  5. 5.

    ZTF21aaqytjr (SN 2021hiz) in UGC 7513

All the SNe Ia listed above have coverage in the g,r,ig,r,i filters beginning from at least two weeks before maximum light and extending beyond +70 days. We note that even with this small volume sample, there are early-type host galaxies like NGC 4382, for which other methods like Cepheid variables are not viable to obtain distances. In this volume, the number of calibrator SNe Ia is limited by the rate of SNe Ia exploding in the universe. The ZTF calibrator sample within the 20 Mpc volume, accumulated to-date, is however, sufficient to measure H0H_{0} to ∼3%\sim 3\% accuracy using only HST for TRGB observations. In our analyses, we only infer the SN Ia light-curve parameters using gg and rr filters since SALT2 is not optimal for redder wavebands. Recently, improved SNe Ia models, e.g. SALT3 [36], and / or BayeSN [42, 63] have been demonstrated to enable an accurate use of redder wavebands e.g. the ZTF ii-band. In future work, we will implement these models trained with high-cadence ZTF SN Ia data in the g,r,ig,r,i wavebands to measure SN Ia distances. It has been demonstrated that the improved SN Ia models can reduce the SN Ia intrinsic scatter to ≲0.1\lesssim 0.1 mag [42, e.g., see]. We nominally expect the σint\sigma_{\rm int} of a similar level when retraining the ZTF calibrator and Hubble flow samples with improved lightcurve models (as assumed for Table 2 We note that our Hubble flow sample has only ∼\sim 100 SNe Ia. This is due to two strict cuts. We apply both the restriction on a host spectroscopic redshift and the limit at the volume of z≤0.06z\leq 0.06. The entire DR1 sample contains >750>750 SNe Ia [16], which is a significantly larger sample than the current Hubble flow rung in the literature. We have also shown here that H0H_{0} inferred from the complete host spectroscopic redshift sample of SNe Ia , with a median z=0.057z=0.057, is consistent with our volume limited subsample. The complete phase-I of ZTF operations has well-sampled lightcurves of ∼3000\sim 3000 of which ∼650\sim 650 are within the z≤0.06z\leq 0.06 volume. These have been discussed in Dhawan et al. [16] and will be presented in future work as part of the ZTF second data release (DR2; Smith et al. in prep). As discussed above, for the current work the Hubble flow sample is not the limiting factor in the final uncertainty on H0H_{0}. However, going forwards the Hubble flow sample will be significantly augmented, both in terms of numbers and the maximum redshift to mitigate the impact peculiar velocity uncertainties [49, e.g., as demonstrated in ]. We summarise the forecast uncertainties in Table 2.

Future TRGB observations with the near infrared camera (NIRCam) on JWST can extend the calibrator sample volume out to larger distances of up to 80 Mpc. In the volume 20<DL<8020<D_{L}<80  Mpc, we have high-cadence light curves of 106 more SNe Ia already obtained (see Figure 4), expected to increase by the end of ZTF. Therefore, the complete sample of ZTF SNe Ia in a volume where JWST observations are feasible can increase the current calibrator sample by a factor of ∼2−3\sim 2-3. We emphasize that current SN Ia cosmology requires cross-calibrating several heterogeneous photometric systems [7]. To get to percent level precision, it is an important cross-check to have observations of a large sample of SNe Ia on a single photometric system, that is the same for calibrator and Hubble flow SNe Ia.

While other concluded and/or ongoing SN Ia surveys have also observed SNe Ia in the distance range feasible for JWST, ZTF has two key advantages. Firstly, the prospective calibrator sample of ZTF is ∼\sim factor two larger in the same volume, since other surveys typically have ∼50−60\sim 50-60 SNe Ia in the specific distance range. This is important to increase the statistical power in the calibrator dataset compared to the current calibrator sample. Secondly, there is a sizable Hubble flow sample of ∼3000\sim 3000 SNe Ia, with a maximum redshift of z=0.1z=0.1 [as discussed in 16, and Smith et al. in preparation for the second data release] on the same photometric system as the calibrator sample, allowing us to reduce systematic errors both from cross-calibration uncertainties and dependence on the host galaxy environment.

In addition to the improvements in the second and third rungs via the single system SN Ia sample proposed here, we would also expect improvements in the absolute calibration of the TRGB magnitude from a combination of multiple primary anchors. For the MW, an increase number of observations and a new full-scale astrometric solution in Gaia DR3 (and subsequently, DR4), compared to EDR3 [40] will decrease the random and systematic errors. Moreover, potential improvements in the extinction maps and primary distance calibration can also decrease the systematic errors in the calibration of the TRGB absolute magnitude from the small and large Magellanic clouds compared to current measurements [30]. For NGC4258, with the maser distance, the current error budget in Jang et al. [32] is conservative. Improvements in the zeropoint of the F814W filter and its EE correction as well as new observations of multiple halo fields of NGC4258 [30] can appreciably reduce the systematic error. Assuming a 0.04 mag error in each of the primary calibrations, we expect a calibration of the TRGB magnitude to have a uncertainty of 0.023 mag (Table 2) More anchor galaxies, e.g. Sculptor [64] and Fornax [46], can further reduce the uncertainty on the TRGB zero point, especially with 1% parallaxes in the future [see 21, for details]. Future facilities can also increase the number of maser galaxies to calibrate the TRGB absolute magnitude by observing ideal candidates at significantly larger distances than the current, single calibrator galaxy, NGC 4258. In the case of the improved TRGB absolute magnitude calibration, this uniform distance ladder can measure H0H_{0} at the ∼1.3%\sim 1.3\% level. However, the expected error with the current uncertainty on MT​R​G​BM_{TRGB} would be ∼1.8%\sim 1.8\%, hence, sufficient for an independent TRGB estimate of H0H_{0}, and arbitrating the Hubble tension. Hence, the increased statistical power and reduced systematic uncertainties from a single, untargeted survey, make this an ideal approach to resolve the H0H_{0} tension.
